title: Signals, Noise and Filtering

mentor.name: BAND-2
mentor.character: Will not talk about a filter until you have measured what the noise actually does.

summary: You will take a raw sensor stream and turn it into a decision: sample it without lying about its frequencies, measure its noise, design FIR and IIR filters by hand, read its spectrum with the right window, and pull a delay or a slope out of it. By the end you can diagnose a vibration channel from a real robot arm and say which part of it is signal.

lessons.title: The Grid Under Every Signal
lessons.goal: Build the sample time grid from a sample rate and say how long a record lasts.
lessons.theory:
A signal in this room is two things that always travel together: an array of numbers and the rate at which they arrived. An ADXL345 accelerometer on the wrist of an arm, read over SPI at 400 samples per second, hands you the first half of that pair. The second half lives in your head until you write it down.

The **sample rate** `fs` is in hertz. Its inverse is the **sample period**, the gap between one reading and the next. Sample `n` was taken at `n / fs` seconds after the first one, so the whole grid is `np.arange(n) / fs`. Nothing in the array knows this. Lose the rate and the numbers mean nothing.

The record length follows from the same two numbers: `n / fs` seconds. That is not the last instant on the grid, it is one period more, because the first sample sits at time zero.

Every function in this course takes `fs` as an argument for that reason. A filter written for 400 Hz is a different filter at 1000 Hz, even with the same code.
lessons.task: Write `time_grid(fs, n)` returning the instants of `n` samples as a numpy array, and `record_seconds(fs, n)` returning how many seconds of arm vibration that record covers.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

FS = 400.0

def time_grid(fs, n):
    # TODO: at what instant was each of the n samples taken
    return np.zeros(n)

def record_seconds(fs, n):
    # TODO: how much time does the whole record cover
    return 0.0

t = time_grid(FS, 8)
print("instants", [round(float(v), 5) for v in t])
print(f"sample period {1.0 / FS:.5f} s")
print(f"record of 4000 samples lasts {record_seconds(FS, 4000):.3f} s")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

FS = 400.0

def time_grid(fs, n):
    return np.arange(n) / fs

def record_seconds(fs, n):
    return n / fs

t = time_grid(FS, 8)
print("instants", [round(float(v), 5) for v in t])
print(f"sample period {1.0 / FS:.5f} s")
print(f"record of 4000 samples lasts {record_seconds(FS, 4000):.3f} s")
lessons.hint: `np.arange(n)` counts 0, 1, 2 and so on. Divide that count by the rate to turn it into seconds.

lessons.title: The Level and the Wiggle
lessons.goal: Split a reading into its constant level and its fluctuation, and show the fluctuation survives.
lessons.theory:
A load cell under a gripper reads 1.02 kg with the jaws empty. That 1.02 is not the measurement you care about, it is the tare, the weight of the jaws themselves. What you care about is the wiggle on top of it.

Signal processing calls the constant part the **DC component** and the varying part the **AC component**, borrowed from electronics and used for every kind of signal since. The DC value of a record is its mean. Subtract it and what is left is centred on zero.

This matters more than it sounds. Almost every tool in the rest of this course, the spectrum, the correlation, the RMS, gives a wrong or useless answer when a large constant offset is still sitting under the data. A 1.02 offset with a 0.03 wiggle on top means the offset carries over a thousand times more energy than the thing you want to see.

Removing the mean does not change the shape. The peak to peak distance is identical before and after, which is the cheapest proof that you removed a level and not information.
lessons.task: Write `split_dc(x)` returning the constant `level` and the fluctuation around it. Print the mean before and after so the removal is visible, and check that the peak to peak span does not move.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def split_dc(x):
    # TODO: separate the constant level from what moves on top of it
    return 0.0, x

raw = np.array([1.02, 1.05, 0.99, 1.01, 1.04, 0.97, 1.03, 1.00])
level, ac = split_dc(raw)
print(f"level {level:.4f}")
print(f"mean before {raw.mean():.4f}")
print(f"mean after  {ac.mean():.4f}")
print(f"peak to peak before {np.ptp(raw):.4f} after {np.ptp(ac):.4f}")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

def split_dc(x):
    level = x.mean()
    return level, x - level

raw = np.array([1.02, 1.05, 0.99, 1.01, 1.04, 0.97, 1.03, 1.00])
level, ac = split_dc(raw)
print(f"level {level:.4f}")
print(f"mean before {raw.mean():.4f}")
print(f"mean after  {ac.mean():.4f}")
print(f"peak to peak before {np.ptp(raw):.4f} after {np.ptp(ac):.4f}")
lessons.hint: Compute the mean once into `level`, then hand back that level and `x` minus it. Computing the mean twice works too but says less about what you meant.

lessons.title: How Loud Is It Really
lessons.goal: Compute the RMS of a fluctuation and relate it to the amplitude of a sine.
lessons.theory:
Peak to peak is a bad measure of how strong a fluctuation is, because one spike decides it. The **RMS**, root mean square, asks a better question: what constant magnitude would carry the same energy as this waveform.

The recipe is in the name read backwards. Square every sample, take the mean of the squares, take the square root: `np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x))`. Squaring is what makes the negative half of a wave count instead of cancelling.

For a pure sine of amplitude `A` the answer is always `A` divided by the square root of two, about 0.707 A, whatever the frequency and whatever the phase. That constant is worth memorising, because it is the bridge between a datasheet that quotes peak values and a measurement that gives you RMS.

RMS is only meaningful on the AC part. Run it on a signal that still has its offset and you measure the offset.
lessons.task: Write `rms(x)` and use it on a 2.0 amplitude sine from the vibration channel. Remove the mean first with the split from the previous mission, then print the RMS next to the amplitude divided by the square root of two.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def split_dc(x):
    level = x.mean()
    return level, x - level

def rms(x):
    # TODO: square, average, take the root
    return 0.0

AMP = 2.0
t = np.arange(400) / 400.0
wave = 1.5 + AMP * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 13.0 * t)
level, ac = split_dc(wave)
print(f"amplitude {AMP:.4f}")
print(f"rms of the ac part {rms(ac):.4f}")
print(f"amplitude over root two {AMP / np.sqrt(2.0):.4f}")
print(f"rms with the offset left in {rms(wave):.4f}")

lessons.title: Decibels Are a Ratio
lessons.goal: Express the signal to noise ratio of a channel in decibels from two RMS values.
lessons.theory:
How good is a measurement? Not by how big the signal is, and not by how small the noise is, but by the ratio between the two. That ratio is the **signal to noise ratio**, and because it spans several orders of magnitude on a real robot it is quoted in decibels.

For amplitudes and RMS values the conversion is `20.0 * np.log10` of the ratio. For powers it would be ten times the log, because power goes as the square. Getting that factor wrong is the most common decibel mistake and it doubles or halves every number you report.

Some anchors worth keeping: a ratio of 2 is 6 dB, a ratio of 10 is 20 dB, a ratio of 1000 is 60 dB. Zero decibels means the noise is exactly as strong as the signal, which is the point where most detectors stop working.

One decibel value alone means nothing. It is always signal over noise, or output over input, or measured over reference, and if you do not say which, nobody can use your number.
lessons.task: Write `snr_db(signal, noise)` using the `rms` you already have. Report the ratio for a clean channel and for one with ten times more noise, and confirm the difference is close to 20 dB.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def rms(x):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x)))

def snr_db(signal, noise):
    # TODO: a ratio of amplitudes turned into decibels
    return 0.0

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
t = np.arange(2000) / 1000.0
vibration = 0.4 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 37.0 * t)
quiet = 0.004 * rng.standard_normal(t.size)
loud = 10.0 * quiet
print(f"quiet channel {snr_db(vibration, quiet):.2f} dB")
print(f"loud channel  {snr_db(vibration, loud):.2f} dB")

lessons.title: The Staircase Under the Curve
lessons.goal: Compute the voltage of one ADC code and show the quantisation error never exceeds half of it.
lessons.theory:
The converter inside an STM32F4 has 12 bits and a 3.3 V reference. It cannot return 1.7 V. It returns the nearest rung of a ladder with 4096 rungs, and every reading you will ever filter arrived already rounded onto that ladder.

The height of one rung is the **LSB**, the value of the least significant bit: `VREF / (2 ** BITS)`. For those numbers it is about 806 microvolts. Any analog value between two rungs is snapped to the closer one, so the error of a single sample can never be larger than half a rung.

That bound is the whole point. Quantisation is not a mystery, it is a known, bounded, deterministic error, and if half an LSB is already bigger than the effect you are hunting then no filter in this course will save you. You need more bits, more reference precision, or amplification before the converter.

Rounding is the right model here. Some converters truncate instead, which doubles the worst case error and adds a constant bias of half an LSB that no amount of averaging removes.
lessons.task: Write `lsb_volts()` from the reference and the bit count, and `quantise(v, step)` that snaps an array onto the ladder. Print the worst error you measure next to half an LSB and confirm it never goes above it.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

VREF = 3.3
BITS = 12

def lsb_volts():
    # TODO: how many volts is one code of the converter worth
    return 0.001

def quantise(v, step):
    # TODO: snap the analog value onto the nearest rung of the ladder
    return v

step = lsb_volts()
t = np.arange(500) / 5000.0
analog = 1.65 + 1.2 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 9.0 * t)
digital = quantise(analog, step)
error = digital - analog
print(f"one code is worth {step * 1e6:.2f} microvolts")
print(f"worst error seen  {np.abs(error).max() * 1e6:.2f} microvolts")
print(f"half a code       {step * 0.5 * 1e6:.2f} microvolts")
print(f"stays under half a code {bool(np.abs(error).max() <= step * 0.5 + 1e-15)}")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

VREF = 3.3
BITS = 12

def lsb_volts():
    return VREF / (2 ** BITS)

def quantise(v, step):
    return np.round(v / step) * step

step = lsb_volts()
t = np.arange(500) / 5000.0
analog = 1.65 + 1.2 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 9.0 * t)
digital = quantise(analog, step)
error = digital - analog
print(f"one code is worth {step * 1e6:.2f} microvolts")
print(f"worst error seen  {np.abs(error).max() * 1e6:.2f} microvolts")
print(f"half a code       {step * 0.5 * 1e6:.2f} microvolts")
print(f"stays under half a code {bool(np.abs(error).max() <= step * 0.5 + 1e-15)}")
lessons.hint: Twelve bits give two to the twelfth codes. To snap a value, divide by the step, round to the nearest integer, multiply back.

lessons.title: Half the Clock
lessons.goal: Compute the Nyquist frequency of a sample rate and decide which tones a channel can carry.
lessons.theory:
A record sampled at `fs` hertz can only represent frequencies below `fs / 2.0`. That boundary is the **Nyquist frequency**, and it is not a rule of thumb, it is the hard edge of what the numbers are able to say.

The intuition is short: you need at least two samples per cycle to know a wave went up and came back down. One sample per cycle and every sample lands on the same point of the wave, which looks like a constant.

So a channel is defined by two numbers, not one. A wrist accelerometer at 200 samples per second has a Nyquist frequency of 100 Hz. The 12 Hz wheel wobble and the 55 Hz gear tone fit under it. The 120 Hz whine of the motor driver does not, and no amount of clever code will recover it later.

Note the word below. Exactly at Nyquist the phase is undetermined and the amplitude you measure depends on where the samples happen to land, so treat the edge as excluded.
lessons.task: Write `nyquist(fs)` and `representable(f, fs)`, then run the three tones the arm actually produces through them at 200 samples per second so the whine comes back as the only one that does not fit.
lessons.hint: Half the sample rate, and a strict comparison against it. Reuse `nyquist` inside `representable` instead of writing the division twice.

lessons.title: Where the Tone Lands
lessons.goal: Apply the folding formula to predict the apparent frequency of a tone above Nyquist.
lessons.theory:
A tone above Nyquist does not vanish. It **folds** back into the band and appears at a lower frequency, indistinguishable from a real one that was never there.

Where it lands is arithmetic, not luck. Wrap the frequency onto the nearest multiple of the sample rate and take the distance: `k = np.round(f / fs)` and the apparent frequency is `abs(f - k * fs)`. The result always falls between zero and Nyquist.

Run that on a channel sampled at 100 Hz and the pattern shows up: 45 Hz stays at 45, 55 Hz comes back as 45 as well, 95 Hz appears as 5, and 105 Hz appears as 5 too. The spectrum folds like paper at every multiple of half the sample rate.

This is the formula you use before touching hardware. If the datasheet of your driver says it switches at 20 kHz and your ADC runs at 1 kHz, the folding formula tells you which innocent looking low frequency in your data is really the switcher.
lessons.task: Write `alias_freq(f, fs)` with the folding formula and print the apparent frequency of the six tones below at 100 samples per second, so that the pairs that collapse onto the same answer are visible.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def alias_freq(f, fs):
    # TODO: fold the frequency back under half the sample rate
    return f

FS = 100.0
for f in (5.0, 45.0, 55.0, 95.0, 105.0, 155.0):
    print(f"{f:6.1f} Hz appears at {alias_freq(f, FS):6.1f} Hz")
lessons.hint: `k` is how many whole sample rates you have to subtract, and `np.round` picks the nearest one. The absolute value handles the case where you overshot.

lessons.title: The Tone That Became Another
lessons.goal: Show that a 27 Hz tone sampled at 40 Hz produces exactly the same numbers as a real 13 Hz tone.
lessons.theory:
The previous mission predicted the folding. This one proves it, and the proof has to be measured rather than asserted, because a badly chosen demonstration of aliasing shows you nothing but rounding dust.

Sample a 27 Hz vibration at 40 samples per second. The folding formula says it should appear at 13 Hz. Build a genuine 13 Hz tone on the same grid and subtract one record from the other. The difference is not small, it is zero to the last bit the machine has, around 1e-15, which is what the sum of a few floating point multiplications leaves behind.

Two guards make this an honest demonstration and both are in the code. First, print the **peak** of the sampled record: if it is not close to one, the samples landed on the zeros of the wave and the whole comparison is about nothing. Second, print the first few samples: they must look like a wave, not like dust.

Cosines are used on purpose. A sine folded from above Nyquist comes back with its phase inverted, so the records would match in shape but not sign. Cosine is even, so the two records are identical number for number.
lessons.task: Write `sampled_tone(f, fs, n)` returning `n` samples of a cosine at frequency `f`. Use it for the 27 Hz vibration and for a true 13 Hz tone at 40 samples per second, and read the peak, the first samples and the largest difference between the two records.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def alias_freq(f, fs):
    k = np.round(f / fs)
    return abs(f - k * fs)

def sampled_tone(f, fs, n):
    # TODO: n samples of a cosine at f hertz, taken at fs hertz
    return np.zeros(n)

FS = 40.0
F_FAST = 27.0
fast = sampled_tone(F_FAST, FS, 16)
slow = sampled_tone(alias_freq(F_FAST, FS), FS, 16)
print(f"folding says {F_FAST:.0f} Hz will look like {alias_freq(F_FAST, FS):.0f} Hz")
print(f"peak of the sampled 27 Hz record {np.abs(fast).max():.4f}")
print(f"peak of the true 13 Hz record    {np.abs(slow).max():.4f}")
print("first samples of each", np.round(fast[:4], 4), np.round(slow[:4], 4))
print(f"largest difference between them {np.abs(fast - slow).max():.3e}")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

def alias_freq(f, fs):
    k = np.round(f / fs)
    return abs(f - k * fs)

def sampled_tone(f, fs, n):
    return np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * f * np.arange(n) / fs)

FS = 40.0
F_FAST = 27.0
fast = sampled_tone(F_FAST, FS, 16)
slow = sampled_tone(alias_freq(F_FAST, FS), FS, 16)
print(f"folding says {F_FAST:.0f} Hz will look like {alias_freq(F_FAST, FS):.0f} Hz")
print(f"peak of the sampled 27 Hz record {np.abs(fast).max():.4f}")
print(f"peak of the true 13 Hz record    {np.abs(slow).max():.4f}")
print("first samples of each", np.round(fast[:4], 4), np.round(slow[:4], 4))
print(f"largest difference between them {np.abs(fast - slow).max():.3e}")
lessons.hint: The instants are the grid from the first chapter, and a cosine of frequency `f` is `np.cos` of two pi times `f` times those instants.

lessons.title: Choosing the Clock
lessons.goal: Pick the lowest available sample rate that covers the highest frequency of interest with margin.
lessons.theory:
Nyquist gives you the floor, not the answer. Sampling a 120 Hz whine at 241 Hz is legal and useless: you get two samples per cycle, the amplitude you read depends on where they land, and any analog filter in front of the converter has almost no room to work in.

In practice you choose an **oversampling factor** on top of Nyquist. Five to ten times the highest frequency of interest is the normal range for measurement. Below five the anti aliasing filter has to be brutally steep. Above ten you are paying storage and bandwidth for nothing.

And you do not get to choose any number. The rates a device offers are a short list, because they come from dividing a crystal: an MPU6050 gives you 1000, 500, 250 and so on. The real decision is picking the cheapest item on that list that clears your requirement.

When nothing on the list clears it, the honest answer is that this sensor cannot measure that phenomenon. Say so instead of picking the largest and hoping.
lessons.task: Write `pick_rate(f_max, margin, candidates)` that returns the lowest candidate rate reaching `margin` times `f_max`, or `None` when the list cannot do it. Try it on the 120 Hz whine and on a 40 Hz wheel tone with a factor of five.
lessons.hint: Build the list of `usable` rates with a comprehension, then take the minimum. An empty list has no minimum, so answer `None` before asking for it.

lessons.title: The Filter That Has To Be Analog
lessons.goal: Compute the attenuation an RC anti aliasing filter gives at the folding frequency and judge whether one pole is enough.
lessons.theory:
Aliasing happens inside the converter. Once the sample is taken, the folded tone and a real one are the same number, so no filter written in Python can separate them. The only place to stop it is before the sample and hitting, which means resistors and capacitors.

The cheapest anti aliasing filter is a single RC low pass, one resistor and one capacitor, with a cutoff `fc` of one over two pi R C. Its magnitude response is one over the square root of one plus `(f / fc) ** 2`, and in decibels that is `20.0 * np.log10` of that magnitude.

One pole rolls off at 20 dB per decade, which is gentle. With a 100 Hz cutoff feeding a converter running at 1000 samples per second, a tone at 900 Hz that will fold down to 100 Hz and sit on top of your signal is attenuated by only about 19 dB, a factor of nine. If your signal to noise budget needed 40 dB, one pole did not do the job.

The fixes are all outside Python: a steeper analog filter with more poles, or a much higher sample rate so the fold lands far up the slope where the RC has done its work. Choosing between them is the real design decision of this chapter.

lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def rc_gain_db(f, fc):
    # TODO: one pole magnitude, then decibels
    return 0.0

FC = 100.0
for f in (100.0, 500.0, 900.0):

lessons.title: Throwing Samples Away
lessons.goal: Decimate a record with and without a pre filter and measure how much of the signal survives each way.
lessons.theory:
Keeping one sample in every four is called **decimation**, and it is what you do when a 200 Hz log is more data than the link can carry. It is also the fastest way to destroy a measurement, because dropping samples lowers the sample rate, and lowering the sample rate moves the Nyquist edge down onto content that was perfectly legal a moment ago.

The fixture below is a 5 Hz wheel signal with a 45 Hz gear tone on top, sampled at 200 Hz. Decimating by four gives 50 Hz, where 45 Hz folds down to 5 Hz, exactly on top of the thing you wanted, and with inverted sign. The RMS of the record falls from 0.707 to 0.283 and nothing in the numbers says why.

The fix is to filter before you throw samples away, so that whatever would fold is already gone. A running average of four is a crude filter and this chapter will not pretend otherwise, but it cuts the 45 Hz tone to about a tenth and the decimated record comes back near 0.66.

That is the rule for the rest of your life with sampled data: **filter, then decimate**. In that order, and never the other one.
lessons.task: Write `decimate_raw(x, factor)` that just keeps one sample out of every `factor`, and `decimate_filtered(x, factor)` that runs a `factor` long running average first with `np.convolve` before doing the same. Compare the RMS of both against the pure 5 Hz record.

import numpy as np

def rms(v):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(v * v)))

def decimate_raw(x, factor):
    # TODO: keep one sample out of every factor
    return x[:x.size // factor]

def decimate_filtered(x, factor):
    # TODO: average away what will not fit, then decimate
    return decimate_raw(x, factor)

FS = 200.0
M = 4
t = np.arange(800) / FS
pure = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 5.0 * t)
mixed = pure + 0.6 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 45.0 * t)
print(f"pure 5 Hz decimated      rms {rms(decimate_raw(pure, M)):.4f}")
print(f"mixed decimated raw      rms {rms(decimate_raw(mixed, M)):.4f}")
print(f"mixed filtered then cut  rms {rms(decimate_filtered(mixed, M)):.4f}")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

def rms(v):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(v * v)))

def decimate_raw(x, factor):
    return x[::factor]

def decimate_filtered(x, factor):
    smooth = np.convolve(x, np.ones(factor) / factor, mode="same")
    return smooth[::factor]

FS = 200.0
M = 4
t = np.arange(800) / FS
pure = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 5.0 * t)
mixed = pure + 0.6 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 45.0 * t)
print(f"pure 5 Hz decimated      rms {rms(decimate_raw(pure, M)):.4f}")
print(f"mixed decimated raw      rms {rms(decimate_raw(mixed, M)):.4f}")
print(f"mixed filtered then cut  rms {rms(decimate_filtered(mixed, M)):.4f}")
lessons.hint: A slice with two colons and a step keeps every `factor` sample. For the filtered version call the smoothed array `smooth` and build the weights with `np.ones` divided by their own count.

lessons.title: The Clock That Trembles
lessons.goal: Predict the noise that sampling jitter adds to a tone and confirm the prediction by measurement.
lessons.theory:
Sampling assumes the samples arrive on a perfect grid. On a microcontroller with interrupts they do not: the conversion starts a few microseconds late whenever something else was busy. That wobble in the instant is called **jitter**, and it turns into amplitude noise.

The mechanism is a first order Taylor step. If the sample is late by a small time, the value you get is the true value plus the slope times that delay. So the error is the derivative of the signal multiplied by the timing error, and steep signals suffer more.

For a sine of amplitude `amp` at frequency `f` the RMS of the derivative is two pi `f` `amp` over the square root of two, which gives the prediction `2.0 * np.pi * f * amp * sigma_t / np.sqrt(2.0)`. Frequency is in that product, so the same clock quality is harmless at 5 Hz and ruinous at 5 kHz.

Twenty microseconds of jitter on a 200 Hz tone costs about 1.8 percent of full scale, which is worse than a 12 bit converter. Timing is part of the signal chain, not an implementation detail.
lessons.task: Build the real instants by adding a seeded jitter of 20 microseconds to the ideal grid, sample the tone at both sets of instants, and compare the measured RMS of the difference against the formula.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def rms(v):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(v * v)))

def jitter_noise_rms(f, amp, sigma_t):
    # TODO: slope times timing error, in rms
    return 0.0

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
FS = 2000.0
F = 200.0
amp = 1.0
sigma_t = 20e-6

clean = amp * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * F * ideal_t)
shaken = amp * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * F * real_t)
print(f"measured error rms  {rms(shaken - clean):.6f}")
print(f"predicted error rms {jitter_noise_rms(F, amp, sigma_t):.6f}")
print(f"as a fraction of amplitude {rms(shaken - clean) / amp * 100.0:.2f} percent")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

def rms(v):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(v * v)))

def jitter_noise_rms(f, amp, sigma_t):
    return 2.0 * np.pi * f * amp * sigma_t / np.sqrt(2.0)

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
FS = 2000.0
F = 200.0
amp = 1.0
sigma_t = 20e-6
n = 4000
ideal_t = np.arange(n) / FS
real_t = ideal_t + sigma_t * rng.standard_normal(n)
clean = amp * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * F * ideal_t)
shaken = amp * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * F * real_t)
print(f"measured error rms  {rms(shaken - clean):.6f}")
print(f"predicted error rms {jitter_noise_rms(F, amp, sigma_t):.6f}")
print(f"as a fraction of amplitude {rms(shaken - clean) / amp * 100.0:.2f} percent")

lessons.title: Samples That Arrive When They Feel Like It
lessons.goal: Resample a record with wandering timestamps onto a uniform grid and compare the error against ignoring the timestamps.
lessons.theory:
A USB IMU logs a timestamp with every reading, and those timestamps are not on a grid. If you drop them and treat the array as uniform you have quietly told every tool in this course a lie, and the tools will believe you.

The repair is **resampling**: build the uniform grid you wish you had with `np.arange(stamps.size) / fs`, then interpolate the measured values onto it with `np.interp`. Linear interpolation is enough when the signal is well oversampled, and it costs one line.

The fixture below wanders by two milliseconds around a 200 Hz grid while carrying a 5 Hz tone. Pretending the stamps were uniform gives a worst error of 0.178 out of an amplitude of one. Interpolating brings it down to about 0.018, ten times better, and the residue left is the curvature that a straight line between two samples cannot follow.

One requirement is easy to miss: `np.interp` assumes the timestamps increase. If a driver can hand you readings out of order, sort them first, or the interpolation silently returns nonsense.
lessons.task: Write `to_uniform(stamps, x, fs)` returning the uniform grid and the values interpolated onto it. Compare its worst error against the true tone with the error you get by ignoring the timestamps altogether.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def to_uniform(stamps, x, fs):
    # TODO: build the grid you wish you had, then interpolate onto it
    grid = stamps
    return grid, x

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
FS = 200.0
n = 600
stamps = np.sort(np.arange(n) / FS + 0.002 * rng.standard_normal(n))
measured = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 5.0 * stamps)
truth = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 5.0 * (np.arange(n) / FS))
grid, fixed = to_uniform(stamps, measured, FS)
print(f"ignoring the timestamps, worst error {np.abs(measured - truth).max():.4f}")
print(f"after resampling,        worst error {np.abs(fixed - truth).max():.4f}")
print(f"grid step {np.diff(grid).mean():.5f} s")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

def to_uniform(stamps, x, fs):
    grid = np.arange(stamps.size) / fs
    return grid, np.interp(grid, stamps, x)

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
FS = 200.0
n = 600
stamps = np.sort(np.arange(n) / FS + 0.002 * rng.standard_normal(n))
measured = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 5.0 * stamps)
truth = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 5.0 * (np.arange(n) / FS))
grid, fixed = to_uniform(stamps, measured, FS)
print(f"ignoring the timestamps, worst error {np.abs(measured - truth).max():.4f}")
print(f"after resampling,        worst error {np.abs(fixed - truth).max():.4f}")
print(f"grid step {np.diff(grid).mean():.5f} s")
lessons.hint: `np.interp` takes the instants you want, then the instants you have, then the values you have, in that order.

lessons.title: The Sample That Never Came
lessons.goal: Detect missing samples from the timestamp gaps and report how many readings were lost.
lessons.theory:
Before any of this chapter applies, the record has to be complete. A dropped SPI transfer or a full buffer leaves a hole, and a hole in an array that you treat as uniform shifts everything after it in time without changing a single value.

Gaps are found with `np.diff(stamps)`, which turns instants into intervals. A healthy interval is one over the sample rate. A gap of twice that means one reading is missing, three times means two, and the threshold to raise the alarm sits between: `gaps > 1.5 / fs` catches a single lost sample without firing on ordinary jitter.

From the size of the gap you can say how many samples went missing: round the gap times the rate, and subtract the one interval that was supposed to be there. That count is what belongs in the log, not just the word dropout.

What you do next depends on the hole. One missing sample can be interpolated with the tool from the previous mission. Forty in a row cannot, and any spectrum computed across that hole is fiction.
lessons.task: Write `find_dropouts(stamps, fs)` returning the indices where a gap is larger than one and a half periods and how many samples each gap swallowed. Run it on a record with two holes in it.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def find_dropouts(stamps, fs):
    # TODO: turn instants into gaps and flag the ones that are too wide
    return np.array([], dtype=int), np.array([])

FS = 100.0
stamps = np.arange(40) / FS
stamps = np.delete(stamps, [12, 25, 26, 27])
where, lost = find_dropouts(stamps, FS)
print(f"record holds {stamps.size} samples over {stamps[-1] - stamps[0]:.3f} s")
print("gaps found after index", where.tolist())
print("samples lost in each", lost.tolist())
print(f"total missing {int(lost.sum())}")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

def find_dropouts(stamps, fs):
    gaps = np.diff(stamps)
    where = np.where(gaps > 1.5 / fs)[0]
    lost = np.round(gaps[where] * fs).astype(int) - 1
    return where, lost

FS = 100.0
stamps = np.arange(40) / FS
stamps = np.delete(stamps, [12, 25, 26, 27])
where, lost = find_dropouts(stamps, FS)
print(f"record holds {stamps.size} samples over {stamps[-1] - stamps[0]:.3f} s")
print("gaps found after index", where.tolist())
print("samples lost in each", lost.tolist())
print(f"total missing {int(lost.sum())}")
lessons.hint: `np.where` on the boolean array gives you a tuple, so take its first element. The number of lost samples is the gap in periods, rounded, minus the one period that was legitimate.

lessons.title: A Fixture You Can Trust Twice
lessons.goal: Build a seeded noisy channel so the same code gives the same numbers on every run.
lessons.theory:
Every measurement in this room is going to be compared against another measurement. That only works if the data stops moving, and random noise moves by definition.

The fix is a **seeded generator**. `np.random.default_rng(seed)` builds a stream whose numbers are decided entirely by the seed, so two runs with the same seed produce the same record, bit for bit, on any machine. Calling `rng.standard_normal(n)` on it draws `n` values from a normal distribution with unit standard deviation, which you scale to whatever noise level you want.

Never reach for the older module level functions. They share one hidden global stream, so adding a call in one place changes the numbers somewhere else, and a fixture that changes when you add a print is not a fixture.

The seed is also a knob. Two different seeds give two independent recordings of the same experiment, which is exactly what you want when you need to check that a result was not a fluke of one particular noise realisation.
lessons.task: Write `make_channel(seed, n)` returning a 37 Hz vibration with noise at five percent of its amplitude. Prove that the same seed repeats and a different seed does not.

FS = 1000.0

def make_channel(seed, n):
    t = np.arange(n) / FS
    vibration = 0.4 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 37.0 * t)
    # TODO: add seeded noise at five percent of the vibration amplitude
    return vibration

a = make_channel(7, 500)
b = make_channel(7, 500)
c = make_channel(8, 500)
print(f"seed 7 against seed 7 differs by at most {np.abs(a - b).max():.3e}")
print(f"seed 7 against seed 8 differs by at most {np.abs(a - c).max():.4f}")
print(f"same seed repeats      {bool(np.array_equal(a, b))}")
print(f"other seed is different {bool(not np.array_equal(a, c))}")
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

FS = 1000.0

def make_channel(seed, n):
    t = np.arange(n) / FS
    vibration = 0.4 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 37.0 * t)

lessons.title: Averaging Buys You Root N
lessons.goal: Average blocks of independent samples and confirm the noise falls with the square root of the block size.
lessons.theory:
Averaging `n` independent samples divides the noise by the square root of `n`, not by `n`. That single fact decides most of the trade offs in this course.

The reason is that variances add, not standard deviations. Two independent noise samples of sigma 0.05 sum to a variance of two times 0.0025, so their mean has a sigma of 0.05 over the square root of two. Repeat and the pattern is fixed: to halve the noise you need four times the samples, and to divide it by ten you need a hundred.

That is a harsh exchange rate, and it is what you pay in time. A hundred samples at 1000 Hz is a tenth of a second of lag, which for a balance controller is an eternity. Every filter later in this course is a way of spending that exchange rate more cleverly, never a way of escaping it.

Measure it once yourself and you will stop hoping. Block average a long noise record with block sizes 1, 4, 16 and 64, take the standard deviation of the block means, and compare it against sigma over the square root of the block size.
lessons.task: Write `block_average(x, n)` that trims the record to a whole number of blocks and averages each one. Print the measured spread of the block means beside the predicted sigma over the square root of the block size.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

SIGMA = 0.05

def block_average(x, n):
    # TODO: cut the record to whole blocks and average each block
    return x

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
noise = SIGMA * rng.standard_normal(8192)
for n in (1, 4, 16, 64):
    got = float(block_average(noise, n).std())
    print(f"blocks of {n:3d}  measured {got:.5f}  predicted {SIGMA / np.sqrt(n):.5f}")
lessons.hint: The modulo tells you how many samples do not fit in a whole block. Reshape the rest into rows of `n` and take `.mean(axis=1)` so each row collapses to one number.

lessons.title: The Noise That Averaging Cannot Touch
lessons.goal: Show that averaging leaves a random walk untouched while it cuts white noise by root n.
lessons.theory:
The root n law of the previous mission has one condition printed in small letters: the samples must be **independent**. Real sensors produce noise that is not.

A gyroscope bias wanders. A thermistor follows the temperature of the board. The model for that is a **random walk**: `np.cumsum(step * rng.standard_normal(n))`, where each new value is the previous one plus a small random push. Consecutive samples of a walk are almost identical, so averaging them averages the same value with itself and buys nothing.

Run both through the same block average and the two behave in completely different ways. The white noise falls from 0.050 to 0.006 as the blocks grow to 64. The walk stays flat around 0.155 whatever you do to it.

That is why a datasheet quotes two different numbers, noise density and bias stability, and why longer averaging eventually makes a gyro estimate worse rather than better. Averaging is a tool against one of these two and useless against the other.
lessons.task: Write `random_walk(rng, n, step)` with a cumulative sum, then block average both the white noise and the walk with the same function and print the two spreads side by side.
lessons.hint: A cumulative sum of small random pushes is exactly a walk. Scale the draws by `step` before summing them, not after.

lessons.title: Quantisation Has a Number
lessons.goal: Predict the RMS of quantisation noise from the code size and convert a bit count into a decibel ceiling.
lessons.theory:
Chapter zero showed that the quantisation error of a converter never exceeds half a code. That bound is useful but pessimistic, because the error spends most of its time nowhere near the bound.

Spread the error evenly across one code and its RMS comes out as the code size divided by the square root of twelve, `step / np.sqrt(12.0)`. That twelve is the variance of a uniform distribution over a unit interval, and it is the number you use when you want to add quantisation to a noise budget alongside the sensor noise.

Turn that into decibels and you get the ceiling of the converter: `6.02 * bits + 1.76` decibels of signal to noise, for a full scale sine. Twelve bits give 74 dB, sixteen give 98. That is a ceiling, never a promise: a signal that only uses a tenth of the range throws away 20 dB of it before you start.

When the measured noise of a channel is far above this ceiling, more bits will not help you. When it is at the ceiling, the converter is the limit and the only way forward is more range or more bits.

lessons.title: The Breakdown Point
lessons.goal: Compare how many corrupted samples the mean and the median of a window can absorb before they lie.
lessons.theory:
The mean has no defence. One sample of a window is enough to move it anywhere you like, because every sample enters the answer with the same weight and nothing bounds the contribution of a large one.

The **median** is defined by position rather than by value, so a corrupted sample only moves the answer by one place in the sorted order. It keeps telling the truth until corrupted samples take over half the window, and that fraction is called its **breakdown point**. For a window of `size` samples the number it tolerates is `(size - 1) // 2`.

Watch it happen on eleven samples that should all read 1.0 while a chattering connector rails some of them to 50. With one bad sample the mean already reports 5.45. With five bad samples it reports 23.3, and `np.median(win)` still reports 1.0. At six the median finally flips to 50, because now the liars are the majority and no estimator can help you.

That last row matters as much as the others. A robust estimator is not magic, it has a stated limit, and past that limit it fails completely rather than gracefully.
lessons.task: Write `breakdown_count(size)` for the number of bad samples a median tolerates, and `mean_and_median(win)` returning both estimates. Print the pair for zero to six railed samples out of eleven.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

WINDOW = 11

def breakdown_count(size):
    # TODO: how many liars a median of this size can absorb
    return 0

def mean_and_median(win):
    # TODO: hand back the fragile estimate and the robust one
    return float(win.mean()), float(win.mean())

print(f"a window of {WINDOW} tolerates {breakdown_count(WINDOW)} bad samples")
for bad in range(0, 7):
    win = np.ones(WINDOW)
    win[:bad] = 50.0
    m, md = mean_and_median(win)
    print(f"{bad} railed  mean {m:6.2f}  median {md:6.2f}")

lessons.title: The Detector That Does Not Believe Itself
lessons.goal: Estimate the noise sigma from the median absolute deviation and flag outliers a three sigma rule misses entirely.
lessons.theory:
The usual outlier rule is to flag anything more than three standard deviations from the mean. It has a defect that hides in plain sight: the outliers themselves are inside the mean and inside the standard deviation, so a big enough group of them raises the bar until it is above their own heads. That failure is called **masking**.

The robust version replaces both statistics. Take `med`, the median of the record. Take `mad`, the median of the absolute deviations from it, `np.median(np.abs(x - med))`. Then the noise sigma is `1.4826 * mad`, where that constant is what makes the estimate agree with the standard deviation when the data really is normal.

On the record below, thirty consecutive samples rail to 3.3 V in the middle of a quiet 0.5 V channel. The mean climbs to 0.92 and the standard deviation to 1.00, so the three sigma bar sits at 3.9 and catches nothing at all. The median stays at 0.52, the MAD sigma at 0.057, and every one of the thirty is flagged.

Zero against thirty is the whole lesson. A detector built on statistics that the fault itself can move is a detector that switches off exactly when it is needed.
lessons.task: Write `robust_sigma(x)` using the median absolute deviation, then count how many samples each rule flags at three sigma: the classic one built on the mean and the standard deviation, and yours.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def robust_sigma(x):
    # TODO: median, deviations from it, median of those, then the scale factor
    return float(x.std())

rng = np.random.default_rng(19)
channel = 0.5 + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(200)
channel[80:110] = 3.3
sigma = robust_sigma(channel)
median = float(np.median(channel))
classic = int(np.sum(np.abs(channel - channel.mean()) > 3.0 * channel.std()))
robust = int(np.sum(np.abs(channel - median) > 3.0 * sigma))
print(f"mean {channel.mean():.4f} against median {median:.4f}")
print(f"std {channel.std():.4f} against robust sigma {sigma:.4f}")
print(f"classic three sigma rule flags {classic} samples")
print(f"robust three sigma rule flags  {robust} samples")
lessons.solution:

def robust_sigma(x):
    med = np.median(x)
    mad = np.median(np.abs(x - med))
    return float(1.4826 * mad)

rng = np.random.default_rng(19)
channel = 0.5 + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(200)
channel[80:110] = 3.3
sigma = robust_sigma(channel)
median = float(np.median(channel))
classic = int(np.sum(np.abs(channel - channel.mean()) > 3.0 * channel.std()))
robust = int(np.sum(np.abs(channel - median) > 3.0 * sigma))
print(f"mean {channel.mean():.4f} against median {median:.4f}")
print(f"std {channel.std():.4f} against robust sigma {sigma:.4f}")
print(f"classic three sigma rule flags {classic} samples")
print(f"robust three sigma rule flags  {robust} samples")
lessons.hint: Three lines: the median into `med`, the median of the absolute deviations into `mad`, then scale. The scale factor is the one written in the theory.

lessons.title: The Hum You Did Not Ask For
lessons.goal: Measure the amplitude of one known frequency by projecting the record onto a sine and a cosine.
lessons.theory:
Not all noise is random. A robot arm plugged into the mains picks up 50 Hz. A brushless driver injects its switching tone. These are **periodic interferences**, and to the standard deviation they look exactly like noise: one number, no explanation.

A single frequency can be measured directly without any transform. Multiply the record by a cosine at that frequency and average, multiply by a sine and average, and the two results are the components of the tone along those two axes. Take `np.hypot(a, b)` and you have its amplitude, phase free.

The factor of two in `2.0 * np.mean(x * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * f * t))` is there because a real tone splits its energy between the positive and the negative frequency. Without it every amplitude you report is half of the truth.

The measurement is exact when the record holds a whole number of cycles of that frequency, which is why the fixture is exactly one second long at 1000 samples per second. Chapter four does this for every frequency at once and calls it a spectrum, but the arithmetic is the one you are writing now.
lessons.task: Write `tone_amplitude(x, f, fs)` with the two projections. Measure the 37 Hz vibration, the 50 Hz hum hiding under it, and a frequency where there is nothing, and compare all three against the plain standard deviation of the record.

FS = 1000.0

def tone_amplitude(x, f, fs):
    t = np.arange(x.size) / fs
    # TODO: project onto a cosine and a sine, then combine
    return 0.0

rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
t = np.arange(1000) / FS
channel = (0.4 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 37.0 * t)
           + 0.08 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 50.0 * t + 0.7)

for f, what in ((37.0, "vibration"), (50.0, "mains hum"), (44.0, "nothing there")):

lessons.title: Noise Sold By the Root Hertz
lessons.goal: Convert a datasheet noise density into an RMS figure for a given bandwidth and back again.
lessons.theory:
An accelerometer datasheet does not quote its noise as a number of milli g. It quotes a **density**, micro g per square root hertz, because how much noise you actually get depends on how much bandwidth you let through.

The conversion is `density * np.sqrt(bandwidth)`. An ADXL355 at 25 micro g per root hertz gives 79 micro g over a 10 Hz bandwidth, 250 over 100 Hz, and 559 over 500 Hz. Same chip, same wiring, three answers, and only one of them is right for your robot.

Read backwards it becomes a design tool. If your control loop can tolerate 100 micro g of noise, the bandwidth you are allowed is `(target / density) ** 2`, which is 16 Hz. Now you know the cutoff of the filter you have to design in chapter six, and you know it before writing a line of filter code.

This is also the honest version of the root n law. Averaging reduces noise because averaging is a filter, and a filter narrows the bandwidth. Both statements are the same statement.
lessons.task: Write `noise_rms(density, bandwidth)` and `allowed_bandwidth(density, target)`. Print the noise of the ADXL355 at three bandwidths, then the widest bandwidth that keeps it under 100 micro g.
lessons.hint: One multiplication by a square root, and one square of a ratio. Check the pair against each other: feed the bandwidth you computed back into the first function and you should land on the target.

lessons.title: The Noise Report
lessons.goal: Assemble one function that reports level, spread, robust spread, outlier count and hum amplitude for a channel.
lessons.theory:
A channel is never described by one number. The four missions before this one each produced a different question, and a report that answers only one of them will send you looking for the wrong fault.

The RMS says how strong the fluctuation is. The robust sigma says how strong it is when the worst samples are not allowed to vote. On a record that is mostly noise the two land on the same value. On this one, which is dominated by a 0.4 amplitude tone, the RMS reports 0.33 and the robust sigma 0.41, and that disagreement is itself the information: what is moving this channel is not noise.

The outlier count separates a chattering connector from a noisy amplifier. The hum amplitude at 50 Hz separates a wiring problem from either. And the level, which is just the mean, separates a drifting offset from all of them.

This is the shape of every diagnostic function you will write in the rest of the course: one pass over the record, several independent statistics, and no verdict. The verdict is for the last chapter, once the tools that produce the numbers are trustworthy.

lessons.title: Every Filter Is a Row of Weights
lessons.goal: Express a moving average as a weight vector and apply it with a convolution.
lessons.theory:
A moving average is usually written as a loop over a circular buffer. That hides what it is. It is a **weight vector**, and applying it is a convolution: slide the weights along the record, multiply, add.

Write the weights down and the filter stops being a special case. `np.ones(taps) / taps` is a row of equal weights that sum to one. Any other row of numbers that sums to one is also a filter, and the whole of chapter six is about choosing those numbers on purpose instead of making them all equal.

`np.convolve` does the sliding. Its `mode` decides what happens at the ends: `valid` returns only the positions where the whole window sat on real data, so the output is `taps - 1` samples shorter than the input and contains no invented values.

The weights must sum to one or the filter changes the level of the signal. Divide by the count and a constant input comes out as the same constant, which is the first thing to check on any filter you build.

lessons.title: Poke It and See What Falls Out
lessons.goal: Recover the weights of a filter by feeding it a single impulse.
lessons.theory:
You can find out what a filter does without reading its code. Feed it a **unit impulse**, a record of zeros with a single one in it, and what comes out is the weight vector itself, in order.

That output has a name, the **impulse response**, and it is the identity card of any linear filter. Two filters with the same impulse response are the same filter no matter how differently they are written, and everything else you will measure, the step response and the frequency response, follows from it.

The reason is the definition of convolution: each output sample is a weighted sum of recent inputs, so when only one input is nonzero, the output at each lag is exactly the weight at that lag.

This is a real diagnostic, not a classroom trick. When a vendor gives you a filtered data stream and no documentation, sending a step or a spike through it and looking at the answer is how you find out what they did to your data.

lessons.title: The Step Tells You the Lag
lessons.goal: Measure the delay a symmetric filter adds by finding where its step response crosses half.
lessons.theory:
The impulse response says what the filter is. The **step response** says what it costs you, because the quantity a control loop cares about is how late the answer arrives.

Push a step through a moving average and the output ramps instead of jumping. It reaches half of the final value exactly `(taps - 1) / 2.0` samples after the step, which for nine taps is four samples. That number is the **group delay** of a symmetric filter, and it is the same for every frequency, which is a property worth a lot later.

Finding it in code is one line: `np.argmax(y >= 0.5)` returns the first index where the condition holds, because argmax on a boolean array stops at the first True.

In seconds it is that count divided by the sample rate. Nine taps at 200 samples per second is 20 milliseconds of lag, which a balance loop will feel. Filtering is never free, and this is the invoice.

lessons.title: How Much of Each Tone Survives
lessons.goal: Compare the measured gain of a moving average against its closed form and find the frequency it deletes completely.
lessons.theory:
A filter is best described by what it does to each frequency. For a moving average of `taps` samples that answer is known in closed form, and it is not the gentle slope most people picture.

The magnitude is the absolute value of `np.sin(np.pi * f * taps / fs)` divided by `taps * np.sin(np.pi * f / fs)`. It falls from one at DC, reaches **exactly zero** at the sample rate divided by the number of taps, and then comes back up in ripples that never fall below about a fifth.

Eight taps at 200 samples per second give 0.760 at 10 Hz, exactly 0.000 at 25 Hz, and 0.202 at 40 Hz. The zero is real, not a rounding artefact: the window covers a whole number of cycles of that tone, so it averages to nothing. Measure it by running a tone through and reading the amplitude back, and the two agree to five decimals.

That 0.202 is the reason a moving average is a poor anti aliasing filter. A tone twice past the cutoff is only attenuated by 14 dB, and no choice of length fixes it, because the ripples are a property of a rectangular window.

lessons.title: Putting It Back Where It Belongs
lessons.goal: Remove the group delay of a causal filter by shifting the output and measure the error before and after.
lessons.theory:
A filter running in real time on a microcontroller is **causal**: at sample `n` it has only seen samples up to `n`, so its output is late by the group delay you measured two missions ago. There is nothing to be done about that live.

Offline is a different situation. When you are analysing a recording you already have the future, so you can shift the output back by the delay and compare it against the truth honestly. A 3 Hz tone through a nine tap average at 200 samples per second gives an RMS error of 0.263 against the original when you compare it where it comes out, and 0.021 after the shift. More than nine tenths of what looked like filter distortion was pure delay.

This is also the trap in every before and after plot you will ever draw. Compare an unaligned filtered signal against its input and the filter looks far worse than it is, and worse the lower the frequency you test at.

lessons.title: Two Passes Make a Triangle

Running a filter twice is the same as running one longer filter once, and you can build that longer filter without touching the data: `np.convolve(weights, weights)` gives the weights of the pair.

That exchange, sharper stopband against more delay and more passband droop, is the whole economy of filter design. Chapter six spends the same budget far better by choosing the weights instead of stacking rectangles.

lessons.title: What Happens at the Ends
lessons.goal: Show that convolution invents zeros at the edges and fix it by padding with the edge values.
lessons.theory:
Ask `np.convolve` for a result as long as the input and it has to make something up, because the first window hangs off the front of the record. What it makes up is zeros, and zeros are almost never what your signal was doing before the recording started.

On a channel sitting at a constant 1.2 V, a nine tap average in `same` mode reports 0.667 for the first sample, 0.800 for the second, and only settles four samples in. Anything downstream that looks at the beginning of the record sees a transient that the sensor never produced.

The repair is to extend the record with its own edge values before filtering, `np.full(pad, x[0])` in front and `np.full(pad, x[-1])` behind, with `pad` equal to half the window. Then filter in `valid` mode: the output is the same length as the input, aligned, and the invented samples are the best guess available instead of zero.

It is not free of assumptions either, it assumes the signal was flat before the record. But a flat assumption is defensible, and a silent jump to zero is not.

lessons.title: The Median Keeps the Edge
lessons.goal: Compare a moving average and a median filter on a step corrupted by spikes and measure what each one leaves behind.
lessons.theory:
Every filter so far has been a weighted sum, which makes it **linear**: scale the input and the output scales with it. A median filter is not, and that is exactly why it can do something no weighted sum can.

Run both over a channel that steps from 0 to 1 while three samples are railed to 3 V by a loose connector. The nine tap average smears the step across eight samples and turns each spike into a bump of a third of a volt that lives for nine samples. The nine tap median crosses the step in a single sample and leaves the flat regions at exactly 0 and exactly 1.

The cost is that the median has no frequency response, so nothing you learned in the last four missions applies to it. It cannot be cascaded into a known shape, it cannot be analysed with a gain formula, and on plain gaussian noise it is worse than the average of the same length.

The rule that comes out of this is an order, not a choice: median first against the spikes, weighted average afterwards against the noise. A spike that reaches a linear filter has already spread itself over the whole window.

lessons.theory:
Three tools, three different faults, and no single winner. The only way to choose is to run all of them against a record whose truth you know, which is why every fixture in this course is built rather than loaded.

The channel below carries a 2 Hz motion, gaussian noise at 0.25, and four railed samples. The moving average attacks the noise and smears the spikes. The cascade attacks the noise harder and delays more. The median deletes the spikes and barely touches the noise.

The number that decides is the RMS error against the clean signal, measured away from the ends so that edge effects do not pick the winner for you. Print all four, including the raw record, because a filter that scores worse than doing nothing is a result you need to see rather than hide.

The combination that wins here is the one the previous mission predicted: median first, then average. Order matters, and it is not a matter of taste.

lessons.title: The Whole Comb at Once
lessons.goal: Transform a record into its frequency bins and read the frequency axis that goes with them.
lessons.theory:
Chapter two measured one frequency at a time by projecting the record onto a sine and a cosine. Doing that for every frequency the record can represent, all at once and in a fraction of the time, is the **discrete Fourier transform**.

For a real signal use `np.fft.rfft(x)`, which returns only the non negative frequencies because the negative half is a mirror of them and carries no extra information. A record of `n` samples gives `n // 2 + 1` complex numbers. Their magnitudes come from `np.abs`, and their angles are the phases, which the next chapters will need.

The frequency of each bin is not something you should count out by hand. `np.fft.rfftfreq(x.size, 1.0 / fs)` builds the axis from the record length and the sample period, and it puts the first bin at zero and the last one exactly at Nyquist.

The two arrays always travel together. A magnitude array without its frequency axis is a picture with no scale, and the most common beginner bug in this chapter is plotting the first against nothing at all.

lessons.title: From Bins to Amplitudes

lessons.theory:
The magnitudes that come out of `rfft` are not amplitudes. They grow with the length of the record, so the same tone measured for twice as long reports twice the number, which makes them useless for comparing anything.

The scaling is `2.0 * mag / x.size`. Dividing by the count removes the length. The factor of two is there because a real cosine of amplitude one is made of two rotating halves, one at plus the frequency and one at minus it, and `rfft` only showed you one of them.

With the scaling in place the spectrum becomes readable. A channel built from a 1.2 V offset and tones of 0.4 and 0.08 comes back reporting 1.2, 0.4 and 0.08, and now a number in a bin means something you could measure with a meter.

lessons.title: The Resolution You Bought With Time
lessons.goal: Compute the bin spacing of a record and show that two close tones separate only when the record is long enough.
lessons.theory:
The spacing between bins is `fs / n`, and that number is the **frequency resolution** of the measurement. Because `n` divided by `fs` is the duration, the resolution is one over the length of the record in seconds. Nothing else enters.

Read that again, because it is the fact people refuse to believe: a faster sample rate does not give finer frequency resolution. It gives a higher Nyquist and therefore a wider spectrum, spread over more bins of the same width. Only **time** buys resolution.

Two tones at 20 and 21 Hz make it concrete. Half a second of data gives 2 Hz bins and one peak. One full second gives 1 Hz bins, and there is still one peak, because two tones one bin apart cannot be told from one tone in between. Two seconds gives 0.5 Hz bins and finally two clean peaks, each reporting an amplitude of 1.0.

So the practical rule needs the safety factor: to separate two frequencies you need a record at least twice as long as one over their spacing. If a bearing fault sits 0.4 Hz from the shaft tone, you need five seconds of data, and a faster ADC will not shorten that.

lessons.title: Nothing Is Created and Nothing Is Lost

The transform moves a record into another set of coordinates. It does not add or remove anything, and there is an equality that proves it: **Parseval**.

Once you are in decibels the vocabulary of filters becomes usable. Minus 3 dB is the cutoff, minus 20 dB is a factor of ten, minus 60 dB is where a 16 bit converter stops being able to tell you anything, and a stopband specification is always written this way.

A thermal drift is not periodic, so it has no business in a spectrum. The transform does not know that. It has to describe your ramp using only sines and cosines, and the only way to build a ramp out of sines is to pile up a large amount of everything at the low end.

A spectrum is several hundred numbers and a diagnosis is three. The step between them is **peak picking**, and it is where most of the mistakes in vibration analysis live.

lessons.title: Padding With Nothing
lessons.goal: Zero pad a record to refine where a peak sits and show that it does not separate two close tones.
lessons.theory:
Sticking zeros on the end of a record makes the transform longer, so the bins get closer together. It is tempting to call that better resolution. It is not, and the difference is worth being precise about.

What zero padding does is **interpolate**. The underlying shape of a tone in the spectrum is a fixed curve whose width is set by how long you actually recorded, and padding only samples that same curve at more points. A 20.3 Hz tone measured for one second at 200 samples per second reports 20.0 Hz on the raw grid, and 20.25 Hz after padding by four, much closer to the truth.

What it does not do is separate anything. The pair at 20.0 and 20.5 Hz that merged into one peak in a one second record still gives exactly one peak after padding by eight, at 20.25 Hz, because the two curves overlap and no amount of sampling an overlap unmixes it.

So padding is for reading a peak position more finely and for reaching a convenient transform length. Resolution still costs time, and that has not changed since two missions ago.

lessons.goal: Assemble detrend, transform, scaling and peak picking into one function that reports what a channel contains.
lessons.theory:
The five previous missions each produced one piece. Put them in the right order and you have the tool that the rest of the course uses: give it a record and a sample rate, get back a list of what is in it.

The order is not negotiable. Detrend first, because a drift pollutes every bin and would win the peak ranking. Transform second. Scale third, so the numbers come out in the units of the sensor. Pick peaks last, on the scaled amplitudes, with a floor chosen from the noise level rather than from taste.

The channel below carries a 1.8 V offset, a slow drift, a 24 Hz shaft tone, a 96 Hz mesh tone, a 288 Hz harmonic and noise. A correct report names the three tones with their amplitudes and does not mention the drift or the offset at all.

That last part is the test. A spectrum tool that reports the offset as the loudest component of the machine is technically right and operationally useless, and this is the chapter where you stop building those.

lessons.title: The Tone That Smeared
lessons.goal: Measure how much of a tone escapes its own bin when its frequency does not land on the grid.

The transform assumes the record repeats forever. Cut one second out of a 20 Hz tone and the ends join perfectly, twenty whole cycles, and the spectrum is a single bin. Cut the same second out of a 20.5 Hz tone and the two ends do not meet: the loop has a step in it, and a step is broadband.

That is **spectral leakage**. The energy that cannot fit in one bin spills into all the others, falling off slowly as one over the distance. The peak itself reads 0.643 instead of 1.0, so both the frequency and the amplitude you report are wrong.

Measure it as a fraction. Add the squared amplitudes of the peak and its two neighbours, divide by the total, and subtract from one. The on grid tone leaves 0.00 percent outside those three bins. The off grid tone leaves 14.09 percent, spread across the whole spectrum where it will sit on top of anything smaller.

There is no way to arrange for every tone to land on the grid, because you do not know the frequencies in advance, which is the whole reason you are transforming. The rest of this chapter is about making the spill fall off faster instead of trying to avoid it.

lessons.title: The Glass Called Hann
lessons.goal: Build a Hann window and apply it to a record so the ends of the loop meet smoothly.
lessons.theory:
Leakage comes from the discontinuity where the end of the record meets its beginning. The cure is to fade both ends to zero before transforming, so there is nothing left to be discontinuous.

The curve that does the fading is a **window**, and the workhorse is the **Hann** window: `0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * np.arange(n) / (n - 1))`. It starts at zero, rises to one in the middle, and comes back to zero, one raised cosine over the whole record.

Applying it is a multiplication sample by sample, not a convolution. You are changing the record, on purpose, before you look at it, and every number that comes out afterwards is a number about the windowed record rather than the original. The next two missions are about undoing that damage in the two different ways it needs undoing.

Do not use the `n` divided by `n` version you will see in some code. The `n - 1` denominator makes the window symmetric, which is what you want for analysis, and the difference shows up as a small asymmetry in the phase you are about to measure.

lessons.title: Windows Steal Amplitude

The Hann window sets half of your record to something close to zero, so the tone that comes out the other side is smaller. Measure a 20 Hz tone of amplitude one through it and the spectrum reports 0.4975. Nothing is broken, you multiplied the signal by a curve whose average is 0.4975.

The off grid tone does not come all the way back. It reports 0.8502, and the missing 1.4 dB is **scalloping loss**: the true peak sits between two bins and neither of them is standing on top of it. Every window has a scalloping loss, the Hann figure is one of the gentler ones, and a rectangular window is worse at 3.9 dB.

So the correction is necessary and not sufficient. If you need amplitudes accurate to better than a decibel from an arbitrary frequency, you need the interpolation two missions from now, not a better window.

lessons.title: Hamming Buys Near and Sells Far
lessons.goal: Compare the near and far sidelobes of the rectangular, Hann and Hamming windows on the same tone.
lessons.theory:
There is no best window. There is a trade, and it runs between how much a window leaks close to the tone and how much it leaks far away from it.

The **Hamming** window is `0.54 - 0.46 * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * np.arange(n) / (n - 1))`, the same shape as Hann with different coefficients chosen to cancel the first sidelobe as far as it will go. It does not reach zero at the ends, and that residue is what limits it later.

Measure both sides on the same 20.5 Hz tone. Near the peak, in the bins three to ten away, the rectangular window leaks at minus 14.5 dB, Hann at minus 40.3 and Hamming at minus 42.0. Far away, past forty bins, Hann has fallen to minus 107 dB while Hamming has stalled at minus 60.2.

So the choice follows the question. Two tones of similar size close together want Hamming. A tiny tone far from a huge one wants Hann. And a rectangular window, which is what you get by not thinking about it, is the worst answer to both questions.

lessons.title: Noise Needs Its Own Correction
lessons.goal: Show that noise through a window scales with the root mean square of the weights, not with their mean.
lessons.theory:
A window takes a different bite out of noise than it does out of a tone, and using one correction for both is a mistake that quietly rescales every noise floor you report.

A tone is coherent across the record, so every sample is scaled and the amplitudes add up in step: the right factor is the mean of the window. Noise is independent from sample to sample, so what adds is the **power**, and the right factor is `np.sqrt(np.mean(w * w))`, the root mean square of the weights.

For a long Hann window those two numbers are 0.5000 and 0.6124, a ratio of 1.22, or 1.76 dB. Report a noise floor with the tone correction and it comes out 1.76 dB too high, every time, on every measurement.

Measure it directly rather than believing me. Noise of RMS 0.0998 through a Hann window comes out at 0.0611, and the prediction from the root mean square of the weights is 0.0612. That is the number to divide by when the thing you are measuring is a floor rather than a peak.

lessons.title: The Weak Tone Beside the Strong One
lessons.goal: Recover a tone sixty decibels below another one, which the rectangular window buries entirely.
lessons.theory:
This is what windows are for. Everything before it was preparation.

The record holds a 20.5 Hz vibration of amplitude one and, fifteen bins away, a 35 Hz tone of amplitude 0.001, sixty decibels below it. That weak tone is a real fault signature: a bearing defect, a loose mounting, a driver harmonic, the things that are small until the day the machine stops.

With a Hann window the skirt falls off as one over the distance cubed and has dropped below the tone by then. The measurement reports 0.000983 against a true 0.001, an error under two percent. Same data, same transform, one multiplication of difference.

lessons.title: Between Two Bins
lessons.goal: Estimate a frequency finer than the bin grid by fitting a parabola through the peak and its neighbours.
lessons.theory:
The grid says 20 Hz. The tone is at 20.3. The information needed to say so is already in the record, and it is sitting in the two bins next to the peak: the one on the side of the true frequency is taller.

One spectrum of a whole record assumes the machine did the same thing throughout. A run up does not: the shaft goes from 10 Hz to 80 Hz, and a single transform of the whole four seconds reports a wide smear that is true and useless.

lessons.title: Averaging Spectra Steadies the Floor
lessons.goal: Average the power of several frames and measure how much steadier the noise floor becomes.
lessons.theory:
The noise floor of a single spectrum is not a floor, it is noise. Each bin is a random number whose spread is as large as its own average, so the picture is a forest of spikes and any threshold you draw across it fires at random.

The fix is to average the **power** of several frames, squared magnitudes, not magnitudes and not complex values. Averaging the complex spectra would cancel the noise and the signal together, because the phases of a tone also differ from frame to frame.

Measure the steadiness as the spread of the floor divided by its average. One frame of white noise gives 1.035, meaning the bins vary as much as they are worth. Eight frames give 0.353, and one over the square root of eight is 0.354. It is the root n law from chapter two, applied to bins instead of samples.

That is the method behind every noise floor you will see quoted properly. It costs record length rather than sample rate, it does not sharpen any peak, and it is what makes a small tone visible above a floor that has stopped jumping.

print(f"one over the root of eight is {1.0 / np.sqrt(8.0):.3f}")

import numpy as np

FS = 400.0

def amplitudes(x, fs):
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(x.size, 1.0 / fs)
    mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x))
    amp = 2.0 * mag / x.size
    amp[0] = mag[0] / x.size
    return freqs, amp

def hann_window(n):
    return 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * np.arange(n) / (n - 1))

def average_power(x, fs, size, frames):
    w = hann_window(size)
    stack = []
    for k in range(frames):
        segment = x[k * size:(k + 1) * size] * w
        freqs, amp = amplitudes(segment, fs)
        stack.append(amp ** 2)
    return np.array(stack).mean(axis=0)

rng = np.random.default_rng(89)
noise = 0.1 * rng.standard_normal(8 * 256)
for frames in (1, 8):
    floor = average_power(noise, FS, 256, frames)
    print(f"{frames} frame(s)  mean {floor.mean():.3e}  spread {floor.std():.3e}  ratio {floor.std() / floor.mean():.3f}")
print(f"one over the root of eight is {1.0 / np.sqrt(8.0):.3f}")
lessons.hint: One character of difference in the append, and it changes what is being averaged. The ratio for eight frames should land within a percent of the last line.

lessons.title: The Ideal Filter Is Infinite
lessons.goal: Build the impulse response of an ideal low pass by sampling a sinc around the middle tap.
lessons.theory:
Ask for the perfect low pass, one that passes everything below the cutoff untouched and deletes everything above it, and the mathematics answers with an impulse response that never ends. That response is a **sinc**, the function `np.sinc`, which numpy defines with the pi already inside it.

Sampled onto a filter of `taps` weights it becomes `2.0 * fc / fs * np.sinc(2.0 * fc * (k - m) / fs)`, where `k` counts the taps and `m` is the middle one, `(taps - 1) / 2.0`. Centring on the middle is what makes the response symmetric, and symmetry is what buys the constant group delay you measured in chapter three.

The centre tap is worth twice the cutoff over the sample rate, 0.2 for a 100 Hz cutoff at 1000 samples per second, and the weights fall away on both sides while changing sign. Those negative weights are not a mistake. A filter that only adds cannot have a sharp edge.

The weights do not sum to one, they sum to 1.0389 here, because you cut an infinite function short. Fixing that is a mission of its own three steps from now, and it is the reason your first hand made filter will have the wrong DC gain.

lessons.title: Cutting It Short Rings
lessons.goal: Evaluate the frequency response of a set of taps and measure the ripple that truncation leaves behind.
lessons.theory:
To judge a filter you need its response at any frequency, not only at the bins of some transform. That is one line: feed the taps a complex exponential and add up the result, `abs(np.sum(h * z))` where `z` is `np.exp(-2j * np.pi * f * k / fs)`.

That expression is what a filter does to a tone, written down. Each tap multiplies a sample from `k` steps ago, a tone `k` steps ago is the same tone rotated by that much phase, and the sum of those rotations is the gain. Run it at zero and you get the sum of the taps, which is the DC gain from the previous mission.

Measure the truncated sinc with it and the ideal filter is not what you built. Across the passband up to 60 Hz the gain wanders between 0.905 and 1.007, a ten percent droop near the corner. Above 150 Hz, where the answer should be nothing, the worst leak is minus 31.8 dB, a factor of forty.

Those ripples are **Gibbs oscillation**, and they are the price of the sharp scissors. Cutting a function short in one domain always produces ringing in the other, which is the same fact that leakage came from in the last chapter, seen from the other side.

lessons.title: Window the Taps
lessons.goal: Multiply the truncated sinc by a Hann window and measure how much the stopband improves.
lessons.theory:
Truncating the sinc is the same as multiplying it by a rectangular window, and by now you know what a rectangular window does. The fix is the one from the last chapter, applied to the taps instead of to the data.

Multiply the ideal response by a Hann window of the same length. The taps near the ends, which were the ones causing the ringing, fade smoothly to nothing. The design becomes `sinc_taps(fc, fs, taps) * hann_window(taps)`, one multiplication.

The stopband goes from minus 31.8 dB to minus 54.7 dB, a factor of fourteen quieter. The passband stops wandering: instead of 0.905 to 1.007 it holds between 0.9988 and 1.0073, well under one percent.

What you pay is the transition. The windowed filter takes longer to get from pass to stop, because the same window that smoothed the ringing also smoothed the edge. That trade is measured in the next mission and it is the one you actually design against.
lessons.task: Write `windowed_taps(fc, fs, taps)` combining the sinc with a Hann window, normalise it, and print the passband range and the worst stopband leak next to the unwindowed figures.
lessons.hint: One line, the product of the two arrays you already have. Both must be built with the same number of taps or numpy will refuse the multiplication.

lessons.title: How Many Taps Do You Need
lessons.goal: Choose the number of taps from a required transition width and verify the width you actually get.
lessons.theory:
Length is the currency of an FIR filter. It buys a sharper transition, and it costs delay and arithmetic, both of which are linear in the number of taps.

The rule for a Hann designed filter, measured between the point where the gain falls to 0.95 and the point where it reaches 0.05, is that the width is about `2.4 * fs / taps`. Turn it around and the design becomes `int(np.ceil(2.4 * fs / width))`, rounded up to an odd number so the filter has a real centre tap and an integer group delay.

Check it on the bench rather than trusting it. Asking for 80 Hz gives 31 taps and measures 79.3. Asking for 50 gives 49 taps and measures 49.8. Asking for 25 gives 97 taps and measures 25.0. The rule holds across a factor of three in length.

You will find other constants quoted, 3.1 and 3.3 among them, and they are not wrong. They measure the width between different levels, usually from the passband edge down to a stated stopband attenuation. Always ask a transition width figure what two levels it runs between.

lessons.hint: Round up with `np.ceil`, turn it into an integer, then add one if it came out even. A 25 Hz transition should ask for 97 taps.

lessons.title: Normalise or Lose the Level
lessons.goal: Scale a set of taps so the DC gain is exactly one and see what the unscaled filter did to a constant.
lessons.theory:
A filter that changes the level of a signal is a filter with a bug, and it is the easiest bug in this chapter to ship without noticing, because everything else about the response looks correct.

The DC gain of an FIR filter is the sum of its taps, which you can see from the response formula at zero frequency: every rotation is one, so the sum of the taps is what is left. The truncated sinc sums to 1.0389, so it makes every reading 3.9 percent larger.

The repair is `return h / h.sum()`. After it, a constant 2.5 V channel comes out at 2.5 V, and the DC gain measures 1.000000 instead of 1.038872. It also rescales the whole response by the same factor, so the passband and the stopband figures you measured before were both 3.9 percent optimistic.

For a high pass the same argument runs at Nyquist instead of at zero, and for a band pass it runs at the centre of the band. The principle does not change: pick the frequency the filter is supposed to leave alone, and make the gain there exactly one.
