lessons.title: Highpass by Inversion
lessons.goal: Turn a low pass into a high pass by subtracting it from an impulse and check both ends of the band.
lessons.theory:
You do not need a second design method for a high pass. Whatever a low pass keeps, the rest of the signal is what a high pass keeps, and subtraction says exactly that.

Build an impulse the same length as the taps with the one at the centre, `delta[h.size // 2] = 1.0`, and return `delta - h`. The impulse is the filter that does nothing, so the difference is everything the low pass threw away. This is **spectral inversion**, and it only works if the low pass is normalised and its centre tap is where the impulse is.

Check the two ends. At DC the gain is 0.000000, because the impulse and the low pass both pass DC at one and they cancel exactly. At 300 Hz, well into the old stopband, the gain is 1.0000, because the low pass contributed nothing there.

The same trick makes a band stop out of a band pass. What it will not make is a filter with a different transition width, because the shape you inverted is the shape you get, mirrored.

lessons.hint: Integer division puts the one on the centre tap of an odd length filter. If the DC gain of your high pass is not zero, the low pass was not normalised.

lessons.title: A Band of Interest
lessons.goal: Build a band pass as the difference of two low passes and check the gain inside and outside the band.
lessons.theory:
A gear mesh tone lives at 140 Hz and everything else on the channel is in the way. What you want is a **band pass**: nothing below 80, nothing above 200, the band between them untouched.

Subtraction again. Take a low pass at the upper edge, take a low pass at the lower edge, and subtract the second from the first. What survives is the difference between what the wide one keeps and what the narrow one keeps, which is exactly the band between the two cutoffs.

Both filters have to be the same length and both have to be normalised, or the subtraction leaves a residue at DC that no amount of staring at the passband will explain. With 101 taps each, the result gives 0.0006 at 30 Hz, 1.0005 at 140 Hz and 0.0000 at 300 Hz.

The transition width of the band pass is the transition width of the two low passes it came from, so a narrow band needs a long filter on both edges. This is the point where an FIR starts costing real time and where chapter seven becomes attractive.

lessons.hint: Build the second low pass at the upper cutoff into `upper` and subtract. The gain at each edge should come out near half, which is what a transition centred on the cutoff means.

lessons.title: Two Taps That Delete a Tone
lessons.goal: Build a comb filter that puts an exact zero on the mains frequency and measure what it costs elsewhere.
lessons.theory:
The cheapest filter that removes a known tone has two taps. Average a sample with the one from half a period of that tone ago, and the two are always opposite, so they cancel: `comb[0] = 0.5` and `comb[delay] = 0.5` with `delay = int(fs / (2.0 * f_hum))`.

At 1000 samples per second and 50 Hz of mains hum the delay is ten samples. The gain is a cosine of the frequency, so the response is exactly zero at 50 Hz and also at 150, 250, 350 and 450, one zero for every odd multiple. That row of zeros is why it is called a **comb**, and for mains interference the harmonics are a gift rather than a problem.

The cost is everything else. The gain at 10 Hz is 0.9511, which is acceptable, and at 30 Hz it is 0.5878, which is not. A two tap comb is a very blunt instrument: it deletes the hum and takes a large bite out of everything within a few tens of hertz of it.

When the signal lives near the hum you need a notch that is narrow instead of cheap, and a filter with a narrow notch and a short impulse response cannot be FIR. That is the argument the next chapter opens with.
lessons.task: Write `comb_taps(f_hum, fs)` for a two tap comb and print its gain at 10, 30, 50 and 150 Hz, then filter a channel carrying a 10 Hz signal plus 50 Hz hum and report the hum amplitude before and after.
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

FS = 1000.0

def tone_amplitude(x, f, fs):
    t = np.arange(x.size) / fs
    a = 2.0 * np.mean(x * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * f * t))
    b = 2.0 * np.mean(x * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * f * t))
    return float(np.hypot(a, b))

def response(h, f, fs):
    k = np.arange(h.size)
    z = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * f * k / fs)
    return float(abs(np.sum(h * z)))

def comb_taps(f_hum, fs):
    delay = int(fs / (2.0 * f_hum))
    comb = np.zeros(delay + 1)
    comb[0] = 0.5
    comb[delay] = 0.5
    return comb

comb = comb_taps(50.0, FS)
print(f"the comb has {comb.size} taps")
for f in (10.0, 30.0, 50.0, 150.0):
    print(f"{f:6.1f} Hz  gain {response(comb, f, FS):.4f}")
t = np.arange(2000) / FS
channel = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 10.0 * t) + 0.3 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 50.0 * t)
clean = np.convolve(channel, comb, mode="valid")
print(f"hum before {tone_amplitude(channel, 50.0, FS):.4f}  after {tone_amplitude(clean, 50.0, FS):.4f}")
print(f"signal before {tone_amplitude(channel, 10.0, FS):.4f}  after {tone_amplitude(clean, 10.0, FS):.4f}")

lessons.title: The Bench Filter
lessons.goal: Design a low pass to a written specification, apply it to a noisy channel and report the improvement in decibels.
lessons.theory:
A filter specification is four numbers and nothing else: the sample rate, the cutoff, how wide the transition may be, and how quiet the stopband has to be. Everything in this chapter turns those four into taps.

The channel below carries a 20 Hz motion at amplitude one, buried under a 300 Hz vibration at 0.8 and broadband noise. The specification says cut off at 120 Hz, transition no wider than 60 Hz, and the stopband under minus 40 dB. Hann gives about minus 55 dB, so the length is decided by the transition alone: 41 taps.

Apply it with an edge padded convolution so the record keeps its length, then measure. The signal to noise ratio, taking the 20 Hz component as the signal and everything else as the noise, goes from minus 0.56 dB to plus 9.52 dB. It does not go higher because the noise that lives below 120 Hz is inside the passband and the filter was never asked to touch it: cutting the band by a factor of four can only buy back the square root of four.

Report the delay along with it. Twenty samples at 1000 per second is 20 milliseconds, and a reader who gets the improvement without the cost has been told half the truth.

lessons.title: A Filter That Remembers Its Own Output
lessons.goal: Implement a one pole recursion and show its impulse response never reaches zero.
lessons.theory:
Every filter in the last chapter looked only at the input. A **recursive** filter looks at its own output as well, and that one change buys an enormous amount of shape for almost no arithmetic.

The smallest one is `prev = a * prev + b * x[n]`, two multiplications and one addition per sample, with a single number of memory. Its impulse response is `b` times `a` to the power `n`: 0.1, 0.09, 0.081, and so on forever. It halves every seven samples and it is still 2.66e-06 at sample one hundred.

That is what the second I in **IIR** means, infinite impulse response. An FIR of the same smoothing power would need dozens of taps and dozens of multiplications. This is why every microcontroller loop in the world reaches for this filter first.

What you give up is symmetry. The response is one sided by construction, so the phase is not linear, the group delay changes with frequency, and none of the alignment tricks from chapter three apply without care. That bill arrives in mission eight.

lessons.title: Where the Pole Sits
lessons.goal: Decide the stability of a one pole filter from its coefficient and count how long it takes to settle.
lessons.theory:
The number `a` in the recursion is the **pole**, and everything about the filter follows from where it sits. Each pass through the loop multiplies the memory by it once more, so the impulse response is a geometric sequence.

Below one in magnitude the sequence shrinks and the filter is **stable**: `abs(a) < 1.0`. Exactly at one it neither grows nor shrinks, and the filter becomes a perfect integrator that will accumulate the smallest offset forever. Above one it grows without limit, and 1.02 is enough to turn an impulse of 0.1 into 5.15 after two hundred samples.

When it is stable, how long it takes to settle is also arithmetic: the response falls to one percent after `np.log(0.01) / np.log(a)` samples, which is 43.7 for a pole at 0.9. Divide by the sample rate for the answer in seconds.

This is not only a filter fact. A pole above one is what a diverging control loop looks like from the inside, and the whole of the balance course is about keeping the poles of a closed loop inside that circle.

lessons.title: Designing From a Cutoff
lessons.goal: Choose the pole of a one pole filter from a wanted cutoff frequency and verify the gain at that frequency.
lessons.theory:
Picking `a` by feel is how most embedded code gets written and it is why nobody can say what the filter does. There is a formula, and it takes one line.

A continuous first order low pass with cutoff `fc` decays with a time constant of one over two pi `fc`. Sampling that decay at intervals of one over `fs` gives a pole of `np.exp(-2.0 * np.pi * fc / fs)`, and the input coefficient is `1.0 - a` so the DC gain is exactly one.

For a 50 Hz cutoff at 1000 samples per second that gives a pole of 0.7304 and an input weight of 0.2696. Push tones through and measure: 5 Hz comes out at 0.9951, 50 Hz at 0.7100 and 200 Hz at 0.2592. The number at the cutoff should be 0.7071, and 0.7100 is minus 2.98 dB against the minus 3.01 you were promised.

That 0.03 dB is the price of the mapping, not a bug. The pole is exact for the time constant and approximate for the corner, and the two drift apart as the cutoff climbs towards Nyquist. Below a tenth of the sample rate the difference is not worth a second thought.

lessons.title: Two Zeros and Two Poles
lessons.goal: Implement the general difference equation with coefficient arrays and check it against the one pole case.
lessons.theory:
One pole gives you one shape. The general recursive filter takes two arrays, `b` for the input samples and `a` for the past outputs, and it can be any shape you can write down.

The difference equation is a sum over each: add `b[i] * x[n - i]` for every input coefficient, subtract `a[j] * y[n - j]` for every output coefficient from one onwards. The entry `a[0]` is by convention one and is what the whole equation is divided by, so it never appears in the loop.

With three coefficients on each side the filter is a **biquad**, two zeros and two poles, and it is the unit that every audio and control library is built from. Anything more complicated is written as several biquads in a row, because a long recursion is numerically fragile while a chain of short ones is not.

Check the implementation before trusting it: give it `b` of one entry and `a` of `[1, -0.9]` and it must reproduce the one pole filter you already have, sample for sample, difference zero.

lessons.title: Phase Is Not Free
lessons.goal: Measure the delay a recursive filter adds at two frequencies and compare it against a symmetric FIR.
lessons.theory:
A symmetric FIR delays every frequency by the same amount, half its length, which is why chapter three could undo the delay with a single shift. A recursive filter cannot do that, and the reason is structural: its impulse response is one sided, so its phase cannot be linear.

Measure it. Take the phase of the input and the output at one frequency, subtract, and divide by the phase per sample. The Butterworth at 50 Hz delays a 10 Hz tone by 4.52 samples and a 30 Hz tone by 4.88. Those are different numbers, and the difference grows as the frequency approaches the cutoff.

The twenty one tap average delays both by exactly 10.0 samples. Longer, and identical, and that is the trade: the FIR costs more delay and gives it back unchanged, while the IIR costs less delay and distorts the shape of anything made of several frequencies.

When does it matter? Any time the shape of a waveform is the measurement: the rise of an impact, the width of a pulse, the relative timing of two channels. When you only care about the amplitude of one tone, it never matters at all.

lessons.title: Filter It Twice, Backwards
lessons.goal: Run a recursive filter forwards and then in reverse to get zero phase, and account for what that costs.
lessons.theory:
Offline you can have the shape of an FIR and the cheapness of an IIR at the same time. Filter the record forwards, reverse it, filter it again, reverse it back: `iir_filter(y[::-1], b, a)[::-1]`.

The second pass delays the record by the same amount as the first but in the opposite direction, so the two delays cancel exactly. Measure it at 10 and at 30 Hz and both come back at 0.0000 samples, not approximately, and that holds at every frequency because the cancellation is structural.

The magnitude is squared, which is the part that catches people. A single pass leaves a 100 Hz tone at 0.2312 and the double pass leaves 0.0535, which is 0.2312 times itself. So the effective cutoff moves down and the slope doubles to minus 24 dB per octave. Design for it by asking for a wider cutoff than you want, or by accepting a filter of twice the order.

And it is strictly offline. The reverse pass needs the end of the record before it can produce the beginning, so this never runs in a control loop. Use it for logs, for calibration, for anything measured after the fact, which is most of what this room is for.

A wheel with a flat spot produces the same bump once per revolution. The spectrum can find that, but there is a more direct question: how far do you have to slide the record along itself before it lines up again.

That is the **autocorrelation**. Remove the mean, then multiply the record by a shifted copy of itself and add, for every shift. `np.correlate` with the full mode gives all the shifts at once, negative and positive, and the half you want starts at index `z.size - 1`, where the shift is zero.

Correlation finds periods that a spectrum finds awkward, because it does not care whether the shape is a sine. A train of sharp impacts spreads across dozens of bins in a spectrum and makes one clean peak here.

lessons.title: Where Did the Echo Come Back
lessons.goal: Locate a known pulse inside a noisy record by correlating the record against the pulse.
lessons.theory:
An ultrasonic transducer sends a burst and waits. What comes back is the burst again, smaller, later, and sitting under the noise of the amplifier. Finding when is the whole measurement.

Correlating a record against a **different** signal is cross correlation, and when that other signal is the thing you transmitted, the position of the peak is the delay. The valid mode of `np.correlate` slides the shorter array along the longer one and returns one value per position, so the index of the largest is the answer directly.

The fixture puts a 192 sample burst at index 37 in six hundred samples of noise with a standard deviation of 1.0, and the burst itself only reaches 0.997. The record peaks at 3.43 somewhere in the noise, so there is nothing to see by eye, and the correlation still lands on 37.

This is the same operation as an FIR filter with the pulse as its taps, which is worth stopping on. Every filter is a correlation against its own impulse response, and every detector in this chapter is a filter you designed by knowing what you were looking for.

lessons.title: The Matched Filter
lessons.goal: Measure the processing gain correlation buys and check it against the length of the pulse.
lessons.theory:
The previous mission found a burst that was invisible. That was not luck, and the amount of help it gives can be calculated in advance.

Correlating against the transmitted pulse is the **matched filter**, and it is provably the best linear detector against white noise. The reason is simple to state: the pulse adds up in step with itself across all its samples, while the noise adds up out of step, so the signal grows with the length and the noise only with its square root.

The gain is `10.0 * np.log10(pulse.size)` decibels, 22.8 dB for a 192 sample burst. Measure it by taking the ratio of the correlation peak to the spread of the correlation away from the peak, and comparing that with the ratio of the pulse to the noise in the raw record. The measurement gives minus 7.3 dB going in, 15.7 dB coming out, a gain of 23.0 against the 22.8 predicted.

That is why sonar, radar, GPS and every ultrasonic range finder transmits a long coded burst instead of a short loud click. Length is free and power is not.

lessons.goal: Refine a correlation peak to a fraction of a sample and turn it into a distance in millimetres.

The correlation grid is one sample wide, and at 100 kilosamples per second one sample of round trip is 1.7 millimetres of range. An echo that truly arrives at 37.4 samples gets reported at 37, and the measurement is 0.7 millimetres short before anybody has made a mistake.

The fix is the parabola from chapter five, applied to the correlation instead of to a spectrum. Three values around the peak, the same vertex formula, and the answer is a fractional lag. Here it gives 37.33 for a true 37.4, and the range goes from 63.46 mm to 64.03 mm against a true 64.14.

That is the honest summary of sub sample interpolation. It is worth doing, it is nearly free, and it stops mattering the moment something physical in your setup is less well known than a fifth of a sample.

lessons.title: Differences Amplify Noise
lessons.goal: Differentiate a noisy record with a plain difference and predict the noise the operation creates.
lessons.theory:
Speed from position, acceleration from speed, rate of change from anything: a robot asks for derivatives constantly, and taking one is where a clean signal goes to die.

The plain difference is `np.diff(x) * fs`, the change between neighbours divided by the sample period. Two independent noise samples get subtracted, so their variances add: the noise of the derivative is `sigma * np.sqrt(2.0) * fs`. Measure it and the error comes out at 13.7, which is the prediction less a little because the difference also attenuates the very high frequencies it is amplifying. The signal to noise ratio of the derivative is about a factor of two, from a record whose own signal to noise ratio was a hundred.

That factor of `fs` is the part people miss. Sampling faster makes the derivative noisier, not better, and the only real defences are the two that come next: use more samples per estimate, or smooth first and pay in bandwidth.

lessons.title: Reach Across Instead of Next Door
lessons.goal: Use the central difference to halve the derivative noise and measure what it costs at high frequency.
lessons.theory:
Comparing a sample with its neighbour uses the shortest possible baseline. Comparing the sample before with the sample after doubles the baseline for the same two measurements, and that is the whole idea of the **central difference**: `(x[2:] - x[:-2]) * (fs / 2.0)`.

The noise halves, exactly. Two samples subtracted still gives the square root of two, but the division by two periods instead of one wins it back twice over: `sigma / np.sqrt(2.0) * fs`, 7.07 predicted against 6.86 measured, half of the forward difference.

The cost is at high frequency. The gain of the forward difference is two `fs` times the sine of half the normalised angle, and of the central one `fs` times the sine of the whole angle. At 5 Hz both give 31.41 against an ideal 31.42. At 300 Hz the ideal is 1885, the forward difference gives 1618, and the central gives 951, barely half.

So the central difference is better when the interesting motion is slow compared with the sample rate, which is almost always. It is worse when you are trying to measure something near Nyquist, which usually means you were sampling too slowly anyway.

lessons.title: Fit a Line and Take Its Slope
lessons.goal: Estimate a derivative by least squares over a window and measure the noise it leaves.
lessons.theory:
Both differences so far use two samples and throw the rest away. Fit a straight line through seven of them instead and take its slope, and you get a derivative that uses every sample in the window.

The least squares slope has a closed form when the samples are evenly spaced. With `k` running from minus three to three, the weights are `k / float(np.sum(k * k))`, which is `k` over 28. Convolve the record with those weights reversed and multiply by the sample rate. This is a **Savitzky Golay** differentiator, the first order case, and it is a fixed FIR filter like any other.

The noise it leaves is sigma over the square root of 28, times the rate: 1.89 predicted against 1.82 measured. Against 13.7 for the forward difference and 6.86 for the central one, the same data gives an estimate seven times cleaner.

Nothing is free. The window is seven samples wide, so the estimate is delayed by three in a causal implementation, and a genuine change in slope inside those seven samples gets averaged. That is the exchange rate from chapter two arriving in yet another disguise.

lessons.title: Order Matters Only When It Is Not Linear
lessons.goal: Show that two convolutions commute exactly while a median and a difference do not.
lessons.theory:
Smooth then differentiate, or differentiate then smooth? For linear filters the question has no content: convolution commutes, and swapping the two stages gives the same array to the last bit. The largest difference between the two orders below is 2.65e-16, which is what a few thousand floating point operations leave behind.

Compare away from the ends: the two orders extend the record differently before filtering, so the first and last few samples disagree for a reason that has nothing to do with commuting.

That is worth knowing because it means the two stages can be merged into one set of weights, which is exactly what the Savitzky Golay differentiator was: a smoother and a difference collapsed into seven numbers.

Put a median in the chain and the equality breaks. Median then difference and difference then median disagree by 0.184 on the same record, and the spike each leaves is different, 0.216 against 0.143. Neither is a bug. They are two different algorithms that happen to be built from the same two parts.

So the rule is: with linear stages, order the chain for numerical convenience. With any nonlinear stage in it, the order is part of the design and has to be chosen by measuring both, on data that contains the fault you care about.

lessons.theory:
The project of this chapter is one channel: an ADXL355 on the wrist of a six axis arm, logged at 1000 samples per second while the arm holds a steady pose. Everything in the room gets used on it.

Nothing else can start until the record is trustworthy. The log arrives as two arrays, timestamps and values, and the timestamps have holes in them where the SPI transfer lost its turn. Every tool from chapter four onwards assumes a uniform grid, and a hole shifts everything after it in time without changing a single number.

So the first stage is the one from chapter one: find the gaps wider than one and a half sample periods, count what they swallowed, then rebuild the grid with `np.arange` and interpolate the values onto it with `np.interp(grid, stamps, x)`.

Report the holes, do not hide them. Three missing samples out of eight thousand changes nothing downstream, and three hundred in a row would make the spectrum of this record a work of fiction. The number belongs in the report either way.

import numpy as np

FS = 1000.0

def wrist_log(seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = 8000
    t = np.arange(n) / FS
    x = 0.35 + 0.02 * t + 0.06 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 50.0 * t + 0.3)
    x = x + 0.20 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 137.0 * t) + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    keep = np.ones(n, dtype=bool)
    keep[[1200, 4001, 4002]] = False
    return t[keep], x[keep]

def repair(stamps, values, fs):
    gaps = np.diff(stamps)
    where = np.where(gaps > 1.5 / fs)[0]
    lost = int(np.sum(np.round(gaps[where] * fs).astype(int) - 1))
    grid = np.arange(values.size + lost) / fs + stamps[0]
    return grid, np.interp(grid, stamps, values), lost

stamps, values = wrist_log(211)
grid, fixed, lost = repair(stamps, values, FS)
print(f"the log holds {values.size} samples over {stamps[-1] - stamps[0]:.3f} s")
print(f"gaps wider than one and a half periods: {int(np.sum(np.diff(stamps) > 1.5 / FS))}")
print(f"samples lost {lost}")
print(f"repaired record {fixed.size} samples on a grid of {np.diff(grid).mean() * 1e6:.1f} microseconds")
lessons.hint: The repaired record is as long as what arrived plus what was lost, and it starts at the first timestamp you actually have. Two lines.

lessons.title: What Is In There
lessons.goal: Produce the peak list of the wrist channel with detrending, a window and correct amplitude scaling.
lessons.theory:
Now the record can be asked what it contains. The order is the one chapter four ended on, with the window from chapter five added: detrend, window, transform, scale, correct for the window, pick peaks.

The window matters here because the tones are not on the bin grid and one of them is small. Without it the 137 Hz mesh leaks a skirt that hides the bearing ring three hundred hertz away, which is exactly the demonstration from chapter five with a real machine attached.

A correct run names four things: the gear mesh at 137.0 Hz with an amplitude of 0.1997 g, the mains hum at 50.0 Hz at 0.0604, and a pair of bins around 317 and 324 Hz at about 0.02, which is not one tone but the ringing of an impact spread over a band.

That last observation is what the rest of the project is about. A peak list is a good report and a bad diagnosis, because it describes a machine as a set of pure tones and a failing bearing does not produce pure tones.
lessons.task: Write `peak_list(x, fs, floor)` that detrends, windows, scales and returns the peaks above a floor, and print the four strongest things in the wrist record.
lessons.hint: Call the detrended and windowed record `shaped` and its transform magnitudes `mag`. The scaling is the usual two over the length, and then one more division by the mean of the window.

lessons.title: Kill the Hum, Keep the Machine
lessons.goal: Remove the mains tone with a zero phase notch and prove the gear mesh came through untouched.
lessons.theory:
The 50 Hz in this record is the building, not the arm. It has to go before anything is measured against a threshold, and it has to go without taking any of the machine with it.

The tool is the recursive notch from chapter seven at a radius of 0.99, which makes the notch about three hertz wide, run forwards and backwards so it costs no delay and no phase distortion. On a logged record that costs nothing, because the whole record is already there.

Measure both halves of the claim, not one. The hum falls from 0.0603 to 0.0004, which is a factor of a hundred and fifty. The mesh at 137 Hz reads 0.1997 before and 0.2000 after, unchanged to the fourth decimal. A filter that only proves the first half has not been tested, it has been admired.

The two tap comb from chapter six would also have deleted the hum. It would have taken 41 percent of anything at 30 Hz with it, and on a machine whose shaft turns at 24 Hz that is the difference between a diagnosis and a wrong one.
lessons.task: Write `clean_hum(x, fs)` that notches 50 Hz with a radius of 0.99 in zero phase, and print the amplitude at 50 and at 137 Hz before and after.
lessons.hint: Two lines: build the coefficients with a radius of 0.99, then run the record through both directions. Every function you need is already above.

lessons.title: Keep Only the Band That Matters
lessons.goal: Isolate the gear mesh with an FIR band pass and confirm what the band kept and what it removed.
lessons.theory:
Trending one number over weeks is how a machine is actually watched, and the number has to mean one thing. The RMS of the whole channel does not: it moves when the mains gets noisier, when the room warms up, when anything at all changes.

The RMS of a **band** does. Build a band pass from 120 to 155 Hz with 201 taps, apply it with the edge padding from chapter three so the record keeps its length, and the result contains the gear mesh and almost nothing else.

Check it with the projection rather than by eye. Inside the band the mesh still reads 0.1997 g, unchanged. The mains hum inside the band reads 0.000008 and the bearing ring at 320 Hz reads 0.000001, both gone to six decimal places. The RMS of the band is 0.1413 against 0.1462 for the whole record, so almost everything left is the tone you asked for.

With 201 taps at 1000 samples per second the filter delays by 100 samples, and the edge padding makes that delay symmetric instead of hiding it. On a trend of one number per record it does not matter at all, which is why offline analysis can afford filters this long.
lessons.task: Write `bandpass(flo, fhi, fs, taps)` and `apply_fir(x, h)`, isolate the 120 to 155 Hz band and report the mesh, the hum and the ring inside it beside the RMS of the band and of the whole record.
lessons.hint: The band pass is one subtraction of two low passes at the same length. For the application build the extended record into `wide` and convolve in valid mode.

value: lowpass(fhi, fs, taps) - lowpass(flo, fs, taps)

lessons.title: Track the Mesh While It Runs Up
lessons.goal: Follow the gear mesh frequency across frames while the arm accelerates, ignoring the fixed mains tone.
lessons.theory:
The record so far was taken at a steady pose. A run up is the other useful test: the joint accelerates and every tone that comes from rotation moves with it, while everything from the building stays where it is.

That is a diagnosis by itself. Split the record into frames of 1024 samples, window each one, and track the strongest peak above 80 Hz. The answers are 105.5, 115.2, 126.0, 135.7, 146.5, 156.3 and 167.0 Hz, a straight ramp, so that tone belongs to the machine.

The lower limit on the search is what makes it work. Without it the 50 Hz mains would win several frames and the track would jump between two unrelated things. Deciding what a peak tracker is allowed to look at is most of what makes one reliable.

A frame of 1024 samples is 1.02 seconds and just under one hertz of resolution. Shorter frames would follow the acceleration more closely and report a wider, less certain peak. That is the same trade as the last five chapters, arriving one final time.
lessons.task: Write `track(x, fs, size, fmin)` returning the strongest frequency above `fmin` in each frame, and print the mesh frequency across a run up from 100 to 180 Hz.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

FS = 1000.0

def hann_window(n):
    return 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * np.arange(n) / (n - 1))

def amplitudes(x, fs):
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(x.size, 1.0 / fs)
    mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x))
    amp = 2.0 * mag / x.size
    amp[0] = mag[0] / x.size
    return freqs, amp

def track(x, fs, size, fmin):
    w = hann_window(size)
    found = []
    for start in range(0, x.size - size + 1, size):
        frame = x[start:start + size] * w
        freqs, amp = amplitudes(frame, fs)
        lo = int(np.argmax(freqs > fmin))
        # TODO: the strongest bin at or above that limit, in hertz
        found.append(0.0)
    return found

rng = np.random.default_rng(213)
n = 8000
t = np.arange(n) / FS
rate = (180.0 - 100.0) / (n / FS)
runup = (0.20 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * (100.0 * t + 0.5 * rate * t * t))
         + 0.06 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 50.0 * t) + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(n))
for k, f in enumerate(track(runup, FS, 1024, 80.0)):
    print(f"frame at {k * 1024 / FS:5.2f} s  mesh at {f:7.2f} Hz")

import numpy as np

FS = 1000.0

def hann_window(n):
    return 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * np.arange(n) / (n - 1))

def amplitudes(x, fs):
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(x.size, 1.0 / fs)
    mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x))
    amp = 2.0 * mag / x.size
    amp[0] = mag[0] / x.size
    return freqs, amp

def track(x, fs, size, fmin):
    w = hann_window(size)
    found = []
    for start in range(0, x.size - size + 1, size):
        frame = x[start:start + size] * w
        freqs, amp = amplitudes(frame, fs)
        lo = int(np.argmax(freqs > fmin))
        best = lo + int(np.argmax(amp[lo:]))
        found.append(float(freqs[best]))
    return found

rng = np.random.default_rng(213)
n = 8000
t = np.arange(n) / FS
rate = (180.0 - 100.0) / (n / FS)
runup = (0.20 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * (100.0 * t + 0.5 * rate * t * t))
         + 0.06 * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * 50.0 * t) + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(n))
for k, f in enumerate(track(runup, FS, 1024, 80.0)):
    print(f"frame at {k * 1024 / FS:5.2f} s  mesh at {f:7.2f} Hz")
lessons.hint: Search only the slice from `lo` onwards and add `lo` back, exactly like the lag search in the correlation chapter. Call the winning index `best`.

lessons.title: The Envelope Says Bearing
lessons.goal: Demodulate the ringing band into an envelope and read the repetition rate of the impacts from its spectrum.
lessons.theory:
The peak list found something around 317 and 324 Hz and could not say what it was. This mission answers it, and it is the one technique in the project that a spectrum alone cannot reach.

A damaged bearing does not produce a tone. It produces a short impact every time the flaw passes the load, and each impact makes the structure ring at its own resonance, here around 320 Hz. So the frequency you can see is the resonance, and the frequency you want is how often the impacts repeat.

The answer is **envelope analysis**, three steps. Band pass around the resonance to keep only the ringing. Take the absolute value, which folds the ringing into a series of bumps at the repetition rate. Low pass at 40 Hz to keep the shape of the bumps and throw the carrier away, remove the mean, and transform that.

The envelope spectrum peaks at exactly 7.00 Hz, with harmonics at 14.12 and 21.12. Seven impacts per second, on an arm whose shaft turns at 24 Hz, is a bearing defect frequency and not a shaft one. That number is the diagnosis, and it was never visible anywhere in the original spectrum.
lessons.task: Write `envelope(x, fs)` with the band pass, the rectifier and the smoother, then print the three strongest peaks of its spectrum below 30 Hz.
lessons.hint: Two lines. Rectify with `np.abs`, smooth with a 40 Hz low pass of 201 taps into `env`, then subtract its own mean so the transform does not report a huge DC bin.

lessons.title: The Whole Room
lessons.goal: Assemble the project into one function that turns a raw wrist log into a written diagnosis.
lessons.theory:
Everything is built. What is left is to put it in one place and let it write the paragraph that a maintenance engineer reads.

The pipeline is the six missions in order: repair the record, detrend it, notch the mains, measure the gear mesh in its band, take the envelope of the resonance band and read its repetition rate. Six numbers come out and each one came from a different chapter of this course.

The rules that turn numbers into words are deliberately dull. Mains above 0.03 g means the wiring needs attention. Mesh above 0.15 g means the gear tone is the dominant motion. An envelope peak above 0.005 g between 5 and 12 Hz means impacts are repeating at a rate that is not the shaft, which is a bearing.

Write the numbers next to the words, always. A report that says bearing fault and nothing else cannot be checked, cannot be trended, and will be ignored the second time it is wrong. A report that says 7.00 Hz at 0.0186 g can be argued with, which is the only kind worth sending.
lessons.task: Write `diagnose(record, fs)` returning the findings as a list of lines, using the hum amplitude, the mesh amplitude in its band and the strongest envelope peak, and print the report.
lessons.hint: Take the envelope of the detrended record, read its strongest peak below 30 Hz into `rate` and `strength`, then append one line per finding with the number first and the word after it.
